items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: So the players that followed me on that were Eddie Shaughnessy and the Sam Woodyard, Billy Cobham, and quite a few drummers after that you know.

ctx.x: How did, I meant to ask this earlier on, but how did the double bass drum set come to fruition? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

Well Eddie Shaughnessy came to me once and he said “hey, did you really start the two bass drums? I thought you did, but did Ray McKinley do it first?” I said well I don’t know because when I was a youngster in 1938 I drew the plans for the double bass drum kit. And around 1940, I saw in Down Beat where Ray McKinley was teamed with Will Bradley. They had a band together. They did a lot of boogie woogie things. And there was a picture of him with just two bass drums, see? And so when I saw Ray after that I said…
It must have helped to be a tap dancer I would think.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think I did a very little bit of A Drum is a Woman. I don't know whether they give me credit. But I know Sam did most of it, Sam Woodyard.

ctx.x: The next hallmark in your career, or at least one of the ones in the mid-’50s, would have been the recording of Duke Ellington’s magnum opus, A Drum is a Woman.
Did they give me credit for doing that? Because most of that, Sam Woodyard did – most of that. I did My People.
So that would have been the ’60s.
